name: NodeMCU DevKit 1.0 (ESP8266)
summary: The open-hardware ESP8266 board that made Wi-Fi projects cheap: an ESP-12E module with USB-serial and breadboard headers.

chip.value: Espressif ESP8266EX in an ESP-12E module

ram.value: About 50 KB of heap and data RAM free for applications (Wi-Fi station connected)

analog.note: 0–1 V at the chip; the board's 220 kΩ/100 kΩ divider gives about 0–3.2 V on A0 (schematic in the NodeMCU repository).

usb.value: Micro-USB via a Silicon Labs CP2102 USB-to-UART bridge

software.note: ESP8266 core for Arduino, maintained by the community.

gotchas.title: Board labels are not GPIO numbers
gotchas.text: The D0–D8 labels on the board are not GPIO numbers: D1 is GPIO5 and D2 is GPIO4 (pin map in the NodeMCU repository).

gotchas.title: Boot-mode pins
gotchas.text: GPIO0, GPIO2 and GPIO15 select the boot mode; parts connected there can stop the board booting.

editorial.history: NodeMCU started in October 2014 as Lua firmware for the ESP8266, and its open-hardware DevKit made the chip easy to use on a breadboard.
editorial.today: Still a cheap way to put a sensor on Wi-Fi. Espressif lists the ESP8266EX as not recommended for new designs, so new projects usually start on an ESP32-C3.
